analysis.one_liner: Makes all wages subject to Social Security payroll tax, ending the cap for high earners.
analysis.headline: The bill died in committee with no vote and no cosponsors; a single Democrat introduced it and the Ways and Means Committee never acted on it.
analysis.plain_summary: Social Security's payroll tax stops applying to each worker's wages above a yearly cap, which was $106,800 in 2011. This bill removes that cap, so everyone would keep paying the 12.4% Social Security tax on every dollar of wages and self-employment income, no matter how much they earn. That money goes straight into Social Security's trust funds, closing a big part of the program's funding shortfall without touching anyone's benefits.
analysis.who_benefits: Everyone who relies on Social Security, now or in retirement, because the program's funding gap narrows substantially. Retired and disabled workers benefit from stronger solvency without any benefit cuts. Working people as a whole gain because the burden falls on the highest-earning households rather than on everyone.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Social Security beneficiaries and future retirees

how_it_helps.text: The bill repeals the ceiling on wages subject to Social Security employment and self-employment taxes (the contribution and benefit base), so high earners pay the tax on wages above the 2011 level of $106,800 [S2].
It applies to both FICA (withheld from employee paychecks) and SECA (self-employment tax), with the change taking effect for remuneration paid after December 31, 2011 [S3].
The bill changes only the tax side, not the benefit formula, so the added revenue extends Social Security's solvency without reducing anyone's checks [S2].
Roughly the top slice of earners pays Social Security tax on all wages instead of stopping at the cap; everyone earning below it pays exactly what they do today [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Households with wage and self-employment income above the cap, roughly those earning more than about $107,000 a year, would pay the 12.4% Social Security tax on all their wages, sharing the cost with employers who pay half. Self-employed professionals like doctors, lawyers, and consultants would pay both halves themselves.

drawbacks.text: The tax increase falls on a relatively small group: households earning above the cap would owe the full 12.4% tax on every additional dollar of wages, a real cost for self-employed professionals who pay both the employee and employer halves [S2][S3].

Removing the cap entirely, rather than phasing it in or raising it, is a blunt approach; critics argue it could discourage high-skill work and push some high earners toward untaxed compensation, and the bill pairs the new revenue with no benefit formula change, so the highest earners pay far more in tax without proportionally higher promised benefits [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The trade is straightforward: a large, permanent improvement in Social Security's finances, paid for by the households best able to pay, in exchange for higher taxes on wages above the cap. Anyone earning under the cap pays nothing extra. The main honest objection is design: it hits self-employed high earners especially hard and gives them no extra benefit accrual on their newly taxed wages. But the stakes for the program's solvency are far larger than those objections.

outcome.mechanism: A single House member introduced the bill in July 2011, it was sent to the Ways and Means Committee, and the committee never held a hearing or vote, so it died when that Congress ended in January 2013.

narrative.text: Rep. Paul Tonko introduced the bill on July 29, 2011 [S1][S5].
It was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means, which holds jurisdiction over payroll taxes, the same day [S5].
No other House member signed on as a cosponsor [S4].
The committee took no further action, and the bill received no hearing, no markup, and no floor vote before the 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Households earning above the payroll tax cap kept paying no Social Security tax on wages above $106,800, and a solution to Social Security's funding shortfall through progressive taxation stayed off the table. The Ways and Means leadership was better off not having to schedule a vote on it.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: High earners above the tax cap

for.name: Rep. Paul Tonko
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to repeal the Social Security payroll tax cap and referred it to committee.

for.name: Social Security advocacy organizations
for.role: Outside supporters of lifting the payroll tax cap
for.what_they_did: Publicly promoted lifting or eliminating the payroll tax cap as the favored progressive fix for Social Security solvency.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee leadership
against.role: Chairs the committee with jurisdiction over payroll taxes
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote on the bill during the two years it sat in committee.

against.name: House Republicans
against.role: Majority party controlling the House and its agenda
against.what_they_did: Did not bring the bill to the floor; lifting the payroll tax cap ran against the party's position against raising payroll taxes on high earners.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken and no other member of either party cosponsored the bill, so the record shows only the Democratic sponsor on one side and committee inaction on the other.

industries.industry: High-income households (wages and self-employment above the cap)
industries.note: They would pay the 12.4% Social Security tax on all wages instead of stopping at $106,800 in 2011. Their interest in keeping the cap intact runs against shoring up Social Security without broad tax increases.
They pay both the employee and employer halves of SECA tax, so removing the cap raises their taxes up to 12.4% on income above the cap.
Employers pay the 6.2% employer half of FICA on all wages under the bill, raising labor costs for firms with highly paid staff.
